messages.content: Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

Job queues with workers and scheduled batch runs solve the same problem — moving work off the request path — but they fit different shapes of work.

A queue with workers suits tasks that arrive continuously and unpredictably: sending emails, processing uploads, generating thumbnails. A producer pushes a job, workers pull from the queue and process it, often within seconds. This gives low latency and lets you scale workers with load. The cost is operational: you must handle retries, dead letters, ordering, and idempotency, since a worker can crash mid-job or a message can be delivered twice.

Scheduled batch runs suit work that is naturally periodic or benefits from processing in bulk: nightly reports, data warehouse syncs, cleanup jobs. A cron trigger starts a run at a fixed time, and it works through a full dataset or table before finishing. This model is simpler to reason about — one run at a time, clear start and end — and works well when a delay of hours is acceptable. The downside is latency: nothing happens between runs, so a job created just after a run has to wait almost a full cycle.

In practice, teams often combine both approaches: a queue handles user-triggered, latency-sensitive work, while a batch scheduler handles aggregate or maintenance tasks that do not need immediate results. The choice comes down to how quickly a job must run and whether it depends on a single record or a full dataset.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

When a queued job fails, the worker usually retries it, often with backoff, since the failure may be transient — a timeout, a locked row, a brief outage downstream. After a set number of attempts, the job moves to a dead-letter queue instead of vanishing, so someone can inspect it and decide whether to fix and replay it or discard it. Because jobs are processed one at a time, one failure doesn't block the others behind it; the queue keeps draining.

A failed step in a batch run behaves differently, because the run is one unit of work moving through a dataset. Some batch systems stop the whole run on the first error, so a bad record partway through blocks everything after it. Others log the failure and continue, producing a partial result that needs a follow-up pass. Either way, recovery usually means rerunning the whole batch (or a resumable checkpoint) rather than retrying a single record. This makes batch failures coarser-grained: fixing one bad row can mean re-running an entire report, not just resubmitting that row.

This difference in failure handling often shapes the tooling choice: queues give fine-grained retry and isolation per job, at the cost of more code to manage state, while batch runs offer simpler operational visibility but a heavier recovery path when something breaks mid-run.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

For a small team, use a queue for anything user-facing and skip the batch scheduler until a real bulk workload shows up. A queue like Redis-backed Sidekiq/BullMQ or a managed service (SQS, Cloud Tasks) handles email, notifications, and file processing with little setup, and it scales down to nothing when idle. Add a scheduler only when you have a genuine periodic job — a nightly sync or report — and even then a simple cron hitting an endpoint is enough; there's no need for a dedicated batch framework at small scale. Avoid running both systems in parallel until the team actually has distinct job types that need them, since maintaining two failure-handling paths costs more than most small teams get back in benefit.
Cut the hedging and commit to the recommendation.
